analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from large social media platforms whose algorithms amplify harmful content.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its October 2021 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Section 230, the law that shields internet platforms from lawsuits over what their users post. Under the bill, a social media company with more than 10 million monthly users could be sued over algorithmic ranking or amplification of content tied to civil-rights violations or international terrorism. Small platforms, transparent sorting like chronological feeds, and basic internet infrastructure such as web hosting would be exempt. It was never considered by the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by algorithmically amplified content — for example, victims of online terrorist recruitment or organized harassment and discrimination campaigns — who today cannot sue the platform that pushed the content to them. Ordinary users of large platforms would also gain more accountability over the recommendation systems that shape what they see.

how_it_helps.text: Removes Section 230 immunity from social media companies with over 10 million monthly users when an algorithm ranks, promotes, or amplifies content directly relevant to claims of civil-rights interference or international terrorism.

Allows civil suits under federal civil-rights statutes (42 U.S.C. 1985 and 1986) and the Anti-Terrorism Act (18 U.S.C. 2333), giving victims a legal path against platforms whose recommendation systems spread the harmful material.

Protects ordinary users' feeds they actually choose: it exempts transparent sorting such as chronological feeds, alphabetical lists, or sorting by user ratings and views, and content a user specifically searched for, so platforms can still offer straightforward tools without new liability.

Exempts small platforms with 10 million or fewer monthly users and internet infrastructure providers such as web hosts and domain registrars, so the new liability falls only on the largest companies running opaque recommendation algorithms.

analysis.who_pays: Large social media platforms — Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Twitter — which would lose immunity from certain lawsuits when their algorithms amplify relevant harmful content, and would face litigation costs, potential damages, and pressure to change how their recommendation systems work. Some of that cost could be passed to users through changes to feeds and product design.

drawbacks.text: The line between covered and exempt ranking is hard to draw in practice: a platform could avoid liability by using only simple, 'transparent' sorting, and platforms would face expensive litigation over what their algorithms did, which smaller companies and their lawyers would bear even when claims ultimately fail.

Critics of narrowing Section 230 argue that broad platform liability encourages companies to remove lawful or unpopular speech rather than risk lawsuits, which could reduce the open forums many ordinary users rely on; this bill tries to limit that risk to civil-rights and terrorism claims, but the threat of litigation would still push platforms toward over-removal of borderline content.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real but limited gains: it targets only the largest platforms and only two categories of serious harm — civil-rights violations and international terrorism — while leaving everyday content-moderation disputes untouched. The cost is greater litigation exposure for a handful of companies and some risk that platforms remove lawful speech to be safe. A reasonable trade on paper, but the scope is narrow and the practical effects of 'algorithmic amplification' liability would have needed careful testing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it went nowhere before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 20, 2021 and on the same day was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever took place; nothing further happened after the referral.
Only two Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large social media platforms are better off, since their Section 230 immunity stays intact and they face no new algorithmic-amplification lawsuits. Ordinary users harmed by algorithmically amplified content got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to strip Section 230 immunity from large platforms whose algorithms amplify harmful content.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Maria Cantwell
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democratic effort with no Republican cosponsors, and it never advanced far enough for any vote that would show the partisan split.

industries.note: These companies would lose Section 230 immunity for lawsuits tied to algorithms that amplify content relevant to civil-rights or terrorism claims, forcing changes to their recommendation systems and exposing them to damages. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the people who would sue them.

They would still face litigation costs defending claims even where the transparent-sorting or search exceptions apply. On the other side, carving out a 10-million-user threshold locks in the current market giants by sparing smaller rivals and any future competitors under that size.
